spoken: Around two hundred and forty BC, a scholar in Egypt worked out the size of the whole Earth.
He didn't travel round it. He used a shadow, a distance and one idea from geometry.
His answer was about two hundred and fifty thousand stadia.
And even today, we can't say exactly how close he came.
This is the story of Eratosthenes, and of a number we still argue about.
Eratosthenes was born around two hundred and seventy-six BC in Cyrene, a Greek city in what is now Libya.
He studied in Athens for years. Then the king of Egypt, Ptolemy the Third, called him to Alexandria.
There he was put in charge of the Library of Alexandria, one of the largest libraries of the ancient world.
The post also made him tutor to the future king.
He wrote about mathematics, geography, poetry, history and the stars.
Admirers called him Pentathlos, like an athlete who competes in five events.
Critics called him Beta, meaning second best at everything.
One thing he didn't need to prove was that the Earth is round.
About a century earlier, Aristotle had pointed to the Earth's round shadow on the Moon during an eclipse.
And he noted that some stars seen in Egypt can't be seen from further north.
Aristotle even reported a size for the Earth, which was four hundred thousand stadia.
Eratosthenes found a way to measure it.
Far up the Nile, on Egypt's southern frontier, lay the town of Syene. Today it's Aswan.
Syene was known for something that happened there once a year.
At noon on the summer solstice, the longest day of the year, upright sticks cast no shadow.
Later writers also tell of a well at Syene, where the noon sunlight reached all the way down to the water.
The Sun was standing straight overhead.
Syene was taken to lie on the Tropic of Cancer, the furthest north the Sun can ever be overhead.
But at Alexandria, on the coast, about five thousand stadia further north, sticks still cast shadows at that noon.
If the Earth were flat, and the Sun far away, sticks in both places would cast the same shadow.
They don't. So the ground between them must curve.
And how much it curves over that distance tells you the size of the whole Earth.
So how big was the shadow at Alexandria?
According to Cleomedes, the shadow was read on a scaphe, which is a sundial shaped like a bowl.
A pointer stands at the bottom, and its tip sits at the centre of the bowl's curve.
At noon, the tip's shadow falls on the inside of the bowl.
The arc from the foot of the pointer to the end of the shadow measures how far the Sun is from overhead.
At Alexandria, that arc was one fiftieth of a full circle.
In degrees, that's seven point two.
It's a small angle, so a stick casts a noon shadow only about one eighth as long as itself.
At Syene, at the same noon, the shadow was nothing at all.
Now here's the key idea. The Sun is so far away that its rays arrive almost parallel.
Draw the Earth, with Syene at the top and Alexandria a little way round.
At Syene, a ray comes straight down the stick. Extend that stick downwards, and it reaches the Earth's centre.
At Alexandria, extend the stick too. It also points to the centre.
There, the ray meets the stick at seven point two degrees.
The Alexandria stick line crosses two parallel lines, which are the ray at Alexandria and the ray down the stick at Syene.
When a line crosses two parallel lines, the alternate angles are equal.
So the angle at the centre of the Earth, between the two cities, is also seven point two degrees.
Syene and Alexandria are one fiftieth of the way round the Earth.
And how parallel are the rays? Between those cities, they differ by less than a thousandth of a degree.
Now he needed the distance between the two cities.
Cleomedes gives it as five thousand stadia.
How was it measured? We don't really know.
Egypt had bematists. These were professional pacers who measured land for farming and for taxes.
Some historians think his distance came from their surveys.
A Latin writer, some six hundred and fifty years later, says royal surveyors measured it.
Either way, if five thousand stadia is one fiftieth of the way round, the whole way round is fifty times as far.
Fifty times five thousand is two hundred and fifty thousand stadia.
From a shadow and a distance, he had the size of the whole Earth.
That's the story as it's usually told. But where does it come from?
Eratosthenes wrote it up in a book, On the Measure of the Earth. The book is lost.
Our main account comes from Cleomedes, who wrote a basic astronomy textbook.
Nobody knows when he wrote it, but it was somewhere between the first century BC and about four hundred AD.
And Cleomedes says himself that his version is simplified.
His account talks about sundials, not the well. The well comes from other writers, like the geographer Strabo.
There's even a second number.
The Roman writer Pliny the Elder gives Eratosthenes' result as two hundred and fifty-two thousand stadia.
Why the extra two thousand? Historians disagree.
Two hundred and fifty-two thousand divides evenly by every whole number from one to ten, but two hundred and fifty thousand doesn't.
Split into three hundred and sixty degrees, it gives a neat seven hundred stadia for each one.
Some think he adjusted his figure to make calculations easier.
Others think he defined a stadion of his own, from the size of the Earth, as Pliny's wording suggests.
So how good was his answer? To check, we need his stadia in kilometres.
A stadion was six hundred feet. But a foot wasn't the same everywhere in the Greek world.
Historians' estimates for the stadion run from about a hundred and fifty to two hundred and ten metres.
The real distance round the Earth, through the poles, is about forty thousand and eight kilometres.
Here's what that range of stadia does to his two hundred and fifty thousand.
With a stadion of about a hundred and seventy-six metres, he's about ten percent too big.
With about a hundred and eighty-five metres, he's about fifteen percent too big.
But take Pliny's two hundred and fifty-two thousand and a short stadion, a hundred and fifty-five to a hundred and sixty metres, and he's within two point four percent.
One study found about a hundred and fifty-seven point seven metres from ancient distances, but critics say it's full of errors.
So the famous claim that he was within two percent depends on choosing a short stadion.
The method itself is sound. If you measure the angle and the distance accurately, it gives Earth's true size.
Cleomedes' version also rests on simplifications. Let's check them.
First, take the parallel rays. That one holds very well, as we've seen.
Second, it assumes that Syene sits exactly on the Tropic of Cancer.
In fact it's a little north of it, by less than a degree. Even there, the noon Sun wasn't quite overhead.
The tropic drifts, too. In Eratosthenes' time it lay about three tenths of a degree further north than today.
Third, it assumes that Syene lies due south of Alexandria, on the same meridian.
In fact it's about three degrees of longitude further east.
And the Earth isn't a perfect sphere, but slightly flattened, by about three tenths of a percent.
Still, the angle came out well. The two cities' latitudes really differ by about seven point one degrees.
What we can't check is the distance, because we don't know his stadion.
Measuring the Earth was only part of what he did.
In his Geographica, he mapped the known world on a grid of parallels and meridians.
It named more than four hundred cities with their locations, and it gave us the word geography.
He measured the tilt of the Earth's axis, and worked out dates in history back to the fall of Troy.
And his name lives on in mathematics, in the sieve of Eratosthenes.
Write out the numbers. Cross out the multiples of two, then of three, then of five, then of seven.
What's left are the prime numbers.
Our earliest record of the sieve was written centuries later, and he may have named it rather than invented it.
Later writers used smaller figures. Ptolemy's Geography, centuries later, used just a hundred and eighty thousand stadia.
Some seventeen centuries after Eratosthenes, Columbus read his work, but chose to believe in an Earth about a quarter smaller.
So here's the whole idea, in one picture.
There's no shadow at Syene, and a shadow of one fiftieth of a circle at Alexandria.
Parallel rays carry that angle to the centre of the Earth.
Fifty times five thousand stadia gives two hundred and fifty thousand stadia round.
How close was he? That depends on a unit we still can't pin down.
But the idea was right, and it measured the whole Earth from two cities in Egypt.
That's not bad for a man his critics called Beta.
